title: Julian of Norwich
hookLine: a woman walled into a cell beside a church, who saw sixteen visions of love

lines: A ROOM ON THE SIDE OF A CHURCH.
cards: A small room is built onto the side of a church in an English city. Stone walls. One little window looks into the church, so you can see the altar.
Another looks out onto the street, so people can come and talk. And a door that, once you've entered, you've promised never to walk out of again.
Some traditions describe a bishop's blessing at the door, and prayers much like those at a funeral. For the rest of your life, this is your world. In Norwich, a woman chose that life.
Today's word is the name for what she became: anchoress.

teach.b: An anchoress, or for a man an anchorite, withdrew from the world to live enclosed in a cell attached to a church. The word goes back to a Greek verb meaning to withdraw. It sounds like a prison.
But anchorites were often respected and sought after, and the street window mattered: people came for advice. We don't even know this woman's real name.
She's probably called Julian because her cell was at the Church of Saint Julian in Norwich. What we know comes mostly from her own book.
In May 1373, when she was thirty and a half, she was so ill that she and everyone around her thought she was dying. A priest held a crucifix before her eyes.
Over the next hours she received a series of sixteen visions, which she called showings. Then she recovered.
She wrote them down in a short version, spent years thinking and praying about what they meant, and wrote a much longer one.
Near its end she tells us that fifteen years and more after the showings, she finally understood.

In Grace Warrack's 1901 version: "Wouldst thou learn thy Lord's meaning in this thing? Learn it well: Love was His meaning." All sixteen showings, the suffering, the strangeness and the comfort, meant one thing.
She wrote in a century of plague and war. She didn't look away from pain. She looked through it, and saw love underneath.

how: Christians, Anglican, Catholic and others, read Julian's Revelations of Divine Love, and her cell in Norwich, rebuilt after wartime bombing, is visited today as a place of prayer.

games.q: for years you've wondered what your sixteen visions meant. at last an answer comes. what is it?
games.why: "Learn it well: Love was His meaning." all sixteen showings, she says, meant love.

practice: Sit where you can see out, a real window, a doorway, or a street pictured in your mind, and watch whoever passes, or picture who might: a neighbor, a delivery driver, a child on the way to school.
Hold each one kindly for a moment, the way an anchoress kept her street window open for whoever came. If you pray, you can pray for them as they pass.

wordCard.voice: Anchoress. A woman who withdrew into a cell beside a church, with one window to the altar and one to the world.

orig.note: Greek: to withdraw, to retire; the root of anchorite and anchoress.

carryVoice: Your line: love was his meaning. Sixteen showings, one meaning. That's day two hundred seventy-one.
